content: Lactobacillus fermentum is a Gram-positive bacterium belonging to the genus Lactobacillus. It is commonly associated with active dental caries lesions and is frequently found in fermenting animal and plant materials, as well as in sourdough. Certain strains of this bacterium are considered probiotics, or friendly bacteria, in animals. At least one strain has been utilized in the treatment of urogenital infections in women. Some strains previously classified as Lactobacillus fermentum, such as RC-14, have been reclassified as Lactobacillus reuteri. Commercially available probiotic strains of Lactobacillus fermentum include PCC and ME-3. Lactobacillus fermentum is widely used in food and feed fermentation processes. Some strains exhibit natural resistance to specific antibiotics and chemotherapeutic agents, raising concerns about their potential role as vectors for transferring antibiotic resistance genes from the environment to humans or animals. This bacterium is also a normal inhabitant of the human intestinal tract, and certain strains have been linked to cholesterol metabolism. To qualify as a probiotic, a microorganism must meet specific criteria, including being of human origin, non-pathogenic, resistant to intestinal transit, and beneficial to the immune system. Lactobacillus fermentum has been identified as a potential probiotic due to its ability to survive the harsh conditions of the digestive system, including low pH levels and high bile concentrations. It has demonstrated the ability to grow and survive in a pH 3 solution and tolerate bile concentrations of 3 g/L, which are comparable to the conditions in the human stomach and upper intestine. Lactobacillus fermentum has shown promise in reducing cholesterol levels. Studies have demonstrated that it can remove cholesterol through mechanisms such as assimilation, binding cholesterol to its cell surface, and incorporating cholesterol into its cellular membranes. Additionally, it may interfere with bile salt recycling, promoting bile salt elimination and increasing the demand for cholesterol to synthesize new bile salts. The strain Lactobacillus fermentum ME-3, discovered in 1994 from human fecal samples, has been identified as an antimicrobial and antioxidative probiotic. ME-3 exhibits strong tolerance to bile and pH fluctuations, surviving pH drops from 4.0 to 2.5 without significant loss in numbers. It has demonstrated the ability to suppress gram-negative bacteria, as well as Enterococci and Staphylococcus aureus to a lesser extent. ME-3 produces antimicrobial compounds such as acetic, lactic, and succinic acids, and putrescine. It has also been shown to prevent spoilage in soft cheese products and positively influence gut microbiota when consumed. Studies in mice have revealed that ME-3 can reduce liver and spleen granulomas caused by Salmonella typhimurium when combined with the antibiotic ofloxacin. Lactobacillus fermentum is generally considered safe due to its association with food and its presence as a normal component of human microflora. It has a low pathogenic potential. Safety studies in mice have shown no adverse effects, such as changes in body weight, feed intake, or clinical signs, when fed Lactobacillus fermentum. Blood biochemistry, including protein, albumin, glucose, and cholesterol levels, remained unaffected, further supporting its safety for use in food. An important safety consideration for Lactobacillus fermentum is the presence of transferable antibiotic resistance genes. For it to be considered a probiotic, it must not harbor such genes, as their transfer could compromise the efficacy of antibiotics. Lactobacillus fermentum has been found to exhibit resistance to amikacin and norfloxacin, which are considered intrinsic resistances common to many lactic acid bacteria. No evidence of transferable or acquired resistance genes has been observed in Lactobacillus fermentum strains. The strain ME-3 has been successfully incorporated into dairy products, where it has demonstrated the ability to suppress foodborne pathogens such as Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., and Escherichia coli, as well as Staphylococcus spp., which are associated with urinary tract infections. In goat milk, ME-3 has been shown to increase the population of beneficial Lactobacilli, further supporting its probiotic potential. Lactobacillus fermentum has also been studied for its heat resistance. It has been identified as a spoilage organism in tomato products, with pectins in tomato juice protecting the bacterial cells from heat destruction. The breakdown of pectin by enzymatic action increases bacterial susceptibility to heat, but natural pectolytic enzymes are often inactivated during heating, allowing Lactobacillus fermentum to remain heat-resistant. Heat resistance is also influenced by the medium in which the bacteria are cultured, with better media enhancing resistance. Lactobacillus fermentum exhibits resistance to certain antibiotics, including vancomycin and tetracycline, as demonstrated by DNA analysis and broth dilution tests. Resistance plasmids for tetracycline and erythromycin have also been identified in some strains. However, Lactobacillus fermentum remains sensitive to other antibiotics, such as gentamicin, cefazolin, penicillin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, ampicillin, carbenicillin, erythromycin, amikacin, and chloramphenicol.
